title: Tackling the XAI Disagreement Problem with Adaptive Feature Grouping
claim: Attribution methods disagree on feature importance when features are treated separately, but agree once interacting features are grouped.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, grouped horizontal bar charts, shared x-axis scale
description: Two side-by-side horizontal grouped bar charts on the California Housing dataset, labeled (a) and (b) below. Each feature row has three blue bars in different shades, one per explanation method (PFI, SHAP, PDP). Panel (a) lists Latitude, Longitude, MedInc, logAveOccup, HouseAge, logAveRooms, Population and logAveBedrms, sorted by importance. The bars for Longitude differ noticeably, from about 0.47 to 0.69, so the methods disagree. Panel (b) merges Longitude and Latitude into one grouped feature, 'Longitude:Latitude'. The three bars for that group are close together, about 0.50 to 0.54, which shows better agreement. Both panels use the same x-axis from 0 to 0.8 and the same dark-to-light blue palette. The eye goes first to the long top bars and the uneven Longitude row in (a).
caption: California Housing. (a) PFI, SHAP, and PDP disagree on the importance of Longitude. (b) By grouping features, we increase agreement between the techniques.
abstract: Post-hoc explanations aim at understanding which input features (or groups thereof) are the most impactful toward certain model decisions. Many such methods have been proposed (ArchAttribute, Occlusion, SHAP, RISE, LIME, Integrated Gradient) and it is hard for practitioners to understand the differences between them. Even worse, faithfulness metrics, often used to quantitatively compare explanation methods, also exhibit inconsistencies. To address these issues, recent work has unified explanation methods through the lens of Functional Decomposition. We extend such work to scenarios where input features are partitioned into groups (e.g. pixel patches) and prove that disagreements between explanation methods and faithfulness metrics are caused by between-group interactions. Crucially, getting rid of between-group interactions leads to a single explanation that is optimal according to all faithfulness metrics. We finally show how to reduce the disagreements by grouping features on tabular/image data.
